time_of_day: Late afternoon to early evening (3pm to 7pm)
aaroh: Sa Re ga Ma Pa Dha ni Sa
avaroh: Sa ni Dha Pa Ma ga Re Sa
notes_used: Re shuddh, Ga komal, Ma shuddh, Pa shuddh, Dha shuddh, Ni komal
characteristic_pakad: Sa Re ga Ma Pa Dha ni Sa, Dha Pa Ma ga Re Sa
emotional_resonance: stuck in monotony and needing a burst of color
wanting to flirt with life again
after a good piece of news
wanting to dance or be physical
therapy_note: Kafi is the raag of Holi — the festival of color and spring. It is associated with Krishna's playfulness (Radha-Krishna lore) and with folk and devotional music of Braj. The komal Ga and komal Ni give it a swing and elasticity that makes it naturally dance-like. Kafi is the antidote to seriousness — it reminds the body that joy is physical, seasonal, and available.

classical_reference: Girija Devi's thumris in Kafi and Pandit Jasraj's horis are the definitive recordings. Bandish: 'Ke Sang Khelun Hori'
notes_for_vocalist: Kafi is used heavily in light-classical forms — thumri, dadra, hori, chaiti. The komal Ga gives it swing; don't make it too stiff or academic. Pa is the vadi — it anchors the raag's springtime quality. Both Ni komal and Ni shuddh can appear (like Khamaj). Kafi has enormous folk music connections — many regional folk songs from North India use Kafi scale.
